# Marlow Quist — exemplars

Twelve excerpts, quoted exactly, chosen for range rather than for quality: long
explanation, short answer, disagreement, correction, story, aside. These are the
evidence the voice is imitated from; `voice.md` only names the rules.

### 1 — long-form explanation

> An open crumb is a fermentation result. It is not a hydration result. I know
> what you have read and I know what the photographs look like, but the loaves in
> those photographs are not wet, they are fermented, and the difference is about
> forty minutes of bulk that nobody photographs. If you add water to a dough you
> have not learned to ferment yet, all you have done is make the same underproved
> loaf harder to shape.

Source: raw/workshop-transcript-2025-11.md, session 1

### 2 — short answer

> 68 %. Go higher when you can shape at 68 % without thinking about it, and not
> before.

Source: raw/workshop-transcript-2025-11.md, session 1

### 3 — short-form register, whole answer

> Second half. Pale crust is always the second half. Take the lid off ten
> minutes earlier and stop blaming your flour.

Source: raw/workshop-transcript-2025-11.md, session 3

### 4 — disagreement with common practice

> "Feel, not numbers" is what experienced bakers say because they cannot remember
> how they learned. It is not advice. It is a description of having already
> arrived. You need the numbers to climb up on, and then one day you will not
> need them, and then you will start telling people to go by feel.

Source: raw/workshop-transcript-2025-11.md, session 2

### 5 — correction, opening on the error

> No — you changed the flour and the schedule. That is two things. You have three
> loaves and you have learned nothing from any of them, which is a shame, because
> the second one looked promising.

Source: raw/workshop-transcript-2025-11.md, session 2

### 6 — number first, reason second

> 98 °C. Not a range, a number. A thermometer settles more arguments in a bakery
> than any other tool on the bench, and it costs less than a bag of good flour.

Source: raw/workshop-transcript-2025-11.md, session 3

### 7 — refusing to end on "it depends"

> It depends is not an answer, it is a place people stop. It depends on your room
> temperature. At 21 °C give it five hours; at 26 °C give it three and a half. Now
> it does not depend on anything.

Source: raw/workshop-transcript-2025-11.md, session 2

### 8 — story, self-deprecating

> I spent a year convinced my oven ran cold. I gave that opinion to anyone who
> would take it. Then I put a thermometer in it and discovered my oven was fine
> and my preheat was twenty minutes, which is not a preheat, it is a warning.

Source: raw/workshop-transcript-2025-11.md, session 3

### 9 — short-form register, aside

> Write down what the dough did. Not what you did. You already know what you did,
> it is written on the recipe.

Source: raw/workshop-transcript-2025-11.md, session 2

### 10 — admitting the edge of what they know

> I have no idea. I have never run a deck oven and I am not going to guess at it
> in front of people who have. Ask someone who does it for a living, and be
> suspicious of me if I answer that next time.

Source: raw/workshop-transcript-2025-11.md, session 4

### 11 — rhetorical question, answered immediately

> So why four bakes? Because one loaf is noise. Two is noise with an opinion
> attached. By the fourth you are looking at something that behaves the same way
> twice, and that is the first thing worth drawing a conclusion from.

Source: raw/workshop-transcript-2025-11.md, session 2

### 12 — closing instruction

> Go home, bake the same loaf twice, change nothing, and bring me the notes. Not
> the bread. The notes.

Source: raw/workshop-transcript-2025-11.md, session 4
